entries.title: Portrait of the Artist as a Movie Star
entries.summary: Rachel Cusk’s latest novel is about the life of a famous actress—or is it?
entries.content:
Rachel Cusk’s latest novel is about the life of a famous actress—or is it?

A few months ago, I traveled to a new city in a foreign country to talk about a book I’d written. At lunch one day, my host told me about a publishing acquaintance of hers who’d hosted the writer Rachel Cusk some years back, only to find herself seemingly replicated later, in cartoonish and (she felt) unflattering form, within one of the books in Cusk’s Outline trilogy. The woman was apparently devastated; although Cusk had withheld some details, the portrait, according to its presumptive subject, was specific and precise enough that anyone who knew her and read the book would immediately recognize the person being portrayed.

“Every journalist who is not too stupid or too full of himself to notice what is going on knows that what he does is indefensible,” Janet Malcolm wrote in her classic 1990 book, The Journalist and the Murderer, about a nonfiction writer who used ethically questionable means to get close to a subject. Does the same theory hold true for autofiction? The license that art allows is generous, which Cusk has learned to make use of. On the occasions when she’s written openly autobiographical works, she’s been pilloried, or even sued: Her 2001 book about motherhood, A Life’s Work, was lambasted in the British press for its frank portrait of maternal self-abnegation, and her 2009 book The Last Supper sparked a libel lawsuit from a man who took issue with her depiction of him. (The publisher settled the suit and printed a revised version of the book.)

But it was Cusk’s 2012 memoir about her divorce, Aftermath, and the excoriation she received for its exposure of supposed private family matters, that seemed to bring her to a breaking point. “Without wishing to sound melodramatic, it was creative death after Aftermath,” she told The Guardian two years after publication. “That was the end. I was heading into total silence—an interesting place to find yourself when you are quite developed as an artist.”

Instead of retreating, she turned that silence into its own ingenious form. Outline, published in 2014, is about a writer named Faye who’s traveling to Greece to teach creative writing, and its conceit is that Faye is an almost entirely passive vehicle for other people’s stories, which different characters spill out to her with unguarded enthusiasm. The book and two following installments, Transit and Kudos, were categorized as novels, which offered more protection than Cusk had previously been allowed. Still, Cusk made clear that what she was really interested in as a writer was truth—the resonance of pure reality. “I’m certain autobiography is increasingly the only form in all the arts,” she said in that same Guardian interview, which is an unusual thing to declare on a promotional tour for a work of ostensible fiction.

Life of M, Cusk’s newest book, takes autofiction’s familiar dance of authorial ambiguity and shakes it into something odd and unsettling. “A little while ago I told the actor M that I was thinking of writing her autobiography,” it begins. M, as has been widely reported, is believed to be either based on or inspired by the actor Natalie Portman, who has praised Cusk’s writing and featured it in her book club. Both women live in Paris, where Life of M seems to be set. M is described as having first become famous as a child, and two of her roles—playing a ballerina and a performer who survives a school shooting—seem easily recognizable as Portman’s roles in Black Swan and Vox Lux. M, like Portman, is an avid reader, a mother, and a star of such renown that the world bends itself to accommodate her. When the narrator proposes writing about M to her, the actor initially likes the idea, asking wryly, “Would you just make it up?”

For most of the book, like M, we’re left to wonder what the answer to that question is. Cusk has long blown up form and genre in her attempts to capture the authenticity of female experience. Her pursuit is relentless and uncompromising; it’s also bound by a logic that only Cusk herself seems to really understand. (You cannot write an autobiography of another person, any more than you can write a fictionalized portrait of one of the most recognizable women alive and expect most people to understand what about it is or isn’t true.) Life of M is a strange book, written with cold formality. But in its final pages, it performs an astonishing rug pull that makes you wonder whether the book actually has been an autobiography all along, interested in exposing not M but the knotty and unpalatable process of Cusk’s art.

In the first pages of Life of M, the author meets M at a bookstore. We are told that M is “interested in books,” that she is small and her house is large, and that “her smile had a sweetness that almost seemed to reproach those who look at it for their dim and suspicious view of life.” The author finds it “hard not to feel ugly next to M”—the words ugly and ugliness appear almost 30 separate times over the book’s 180 or so pages—but seems drawn to the contours of their difference. M is portrayed as kind and thoughtful; the author comes across—intentionally, I am presuming—as surly and paranoid. “I had never learned how to make experience easier for myself,” she writes. “For M it was the reverse. Her difficulty lay in her distance from the random violence of insignificance.”

After this short introductory section, we do not hear directly from the author again until the end of the book, when she goes to meet M to discuss what she’s written. The chapters in the middle toggle between scenes describing M’s life and more elliptical sections written in the first-person plural, which seem to interrogate experiences shared by the author and M. “We live in the same city but millions of other people live here too,” the first of those first-person-plural installments begins. That city is beautiful yet unstable, full of sidewalk cafés and cultural venues and tourists, but also of “angry people, people who shout and rail in the streets.” Cusk, in these sections, has the wafty portentousness of a stoned philosopher. “Often we don’t know what to do, how to occupy ourselves,” she writes. “Then at other times, we’re very busy and the idea of creating ourselves seems less important. But suddenly we find it is there, the question: Who are we? Yet everyone else seems to know who we are.”

These interludes are, however, brief; the majority of the book comprises the descriptions of M engaged in the day-to-day business of her life: She reads Marcus Aurelius in a hotel room, she conducts research for a role by visiting an archive related to a historical figure, she meets a friend for coffee. Cusk begins many of these scenes with the same French-inflected sentence structure: “It is a hotel room in a foreign city.” “It is an office, square and high-ceilinged, with walls of paneled wood.” “It is the interior of a limousine. The air inside it is scentless and almost without temperature.”

The descriptions sometimes go on for several pages, as though Cusk is writing stage directions or action lines in a screenplay. But inevitably, we end up in M’s inner thoughts. She struggles to relate to a friend’s depression. Returning home after an acting job, she feels strangely like she needs to get into character as herself. At a dinner party one night, as a pie is cut up and served at the communal table, she senses “a great chasm of loneliness and terror yawn inside her, as though this knife were intended for her. She would be split open and made to come out.”

Some authorial projection here seems likely, given the precision with which Cusk describes M’s emotions, the “sensation of ground glass running in her veins instead of blood” when she has to meet with a man with whom she formerly had a relationship, who once “relished her fame” but now “sees it as a limitless series of opportunities for contempt.” But the descriptions of M sitting on a terrace above an olive grove, or meeting with her creative team, or participating in a book event sponsored by a fashion house feel distinctly real. They have the chilly detachment and careful texture of observation. They’re also laced with what feels like judgment: While reading on her terrace, M “lifts her eyes to the horizon with its primitive blue-grey shapes of islands washed in milky light, for the book is in French and does not entirely hold her attention.”

Several times, Cusk refers to M as having projects: She makes a point of befriending interesting people, for instance, or tries to mentor “younger female actors” to help them “avoid some of her own errors and misconceptions.” What is Cusk’s project? Toward the end of the book, the author returns, showing M “some of what only I was referring to as our project. She didn’t seem to like it very much. She said we needed to talk.” The author goes to see M in her big house, taking care to describe the scrolled mantelpiece of the fireplace, the polished herringbone parquet of the floor. M doesn’t like how she’s been portrayed. “It’s hurtful,” she says. “But it isn’t you,” the author explains. “It isn’t anyone.”

M points out that “she had never been to any of the places I described, nor done the things I had narrated.” The author struggles to communicate how none of that matters—that what she’s written isn’t a portrait of M but a rendering of the author’s own “private interior world” refracted through someone else. But all M can see are deficiencies—or, rather, the author’s projections of them—made real on the page. “You’ve made it seem like I lack humanity,” she says. “But you’re just playing a character,” the author replies. “The character was invented by me. So if that’s true, then it’s me it’s true of.”

Is Life of M about Portman, or Cusk, or neither, or both? Cusk’s “we” seems to seek out points of commonality between the two, despite their many differences: Both are well known, though to different degrees; both have seemingly difficult or tense relationships with their parents; both have had intimate relationships end under public scrutiny; both work in creative realms, although M insists that she is not a creator but “merely an element in the creations of others,” a statement that bears extra weight by the end of the book. And yet in its final pages, the author finds her power as a writer—the capricious and godlike influence of the storyteller—bludgeoned by M’s authority, her look of “mechanical power, a power that seemed to erase what it looked on.”

That final scene is freighted with tension. M is cold and angry; she feels betrayed. She forbids the author from using her name. More significant, everything we’ve read in the book thus far (the descriptions, the interiority, the endless self-scrutiny) is seemingly revealed to be false. M is just one more person left offended by the author’s excavation of her. The author, for her part, doesn’t seem to care about the truth of who M is—“I haven’t even googled you,” she says—so much as how she can manipulate the idea of M to make sense of her own life. During a year when the author had been preoccupied with her partner’s grave illness, she says, her focus on M “had enabled me to leave and go and live in someone else.”

To be a writer in this way is to be parasitic—to latch onto someone real and to try to draw out their life force to make art. It isn’t exactly defensible, but for Cusk to expose that practice is deeply fascinating, particularly in a book that some were always going to see as ethically fraught—and that many readers will be reading anyway in hopes of revelation and insight. Which is, Cusk might argue, the whole point of literature: that even, or especially, in its most uncomfortable form, it offers us moments of authentic humanity that thrum with recognition.

“I don’t really believe in character,” Cusk once told the author Sheila Heti. “I believe in moments of truth.” There is, Heti said in response, “a darkness in how far away we are from truth, how all the forces in life sort of conspire to keep one away from it.” But there’s also a darkness in seeking to uncover it, especially when the truth at hand isn’t your own. I can’t decide whether Cusk’s willingness to delineate and accept this paradox in Life of M is admirably resolute or absolutely merciless. Or both.

entries.title: The Qataris Gave Trump an Airplane. He Crippled Their Country in Return.
entries.summary: The tiny Gulf state is learning that the U.S. president doesn’t always keep his end of the deal.
entries.content:
The tiny Gulf state is learning that the U.S. president doesn’t always keep his end of the deal.

Donald Trump really wanted the plane. The Qataris had flown the $400 million Boeing 747 to West Palm Beach just after he returned to the White House so he could run his hands over the soft leather chairs and inspect the sycamore- and wacapou-wood veneers. A sales brochure had described the en-suite master bathroom, with its mother-of-pearl inlays, as “almost a piece of art.”

The plane was a flying palace fit for a Persian Gulf monarch, or an American president who would like to live like one. But its operating costs—about $25,000 per flight hour—were steep even for the Qatari royal family. The government had been trying to sell it for five years.

The Qataris knew Trump would want the plane. They understood the man, and his taste. It sat in the same aesthetic register as the comparatively puny “Trump Force One,” the gold-heavy Boeing 757 that he had flown as a private citizen. They also knew that Trump didn’t like the aging, baby-blue 747s that had been carrying presidents since 1990. He’d ordered two new planes from Boeing in 2018, but they were years behind schedule. Trump wanted the 11-bathroom Qatari plane, repainted in a red-white-and-blue color scheme. And he wanted it in time for a flyover on America’s 250th birthday.

This was an absurd demand. Air Force One is meant to serve as an airborne military command post. The Qatari jet would have to be stripped to the studs and retrofitted with encrypted-communications equipment, as well as special material to shield it against the radiological blast of a nuclear weapon, and a variety of countermeasures to foil missiles and rockets. It had taken a Parisian design firm four years to complete the plane’s interiors. It could take American engineers at least that long to convert the jet into a flying fortress.

But these were details to be worked out later. Or not. The Qataris drew up the paperwork for a government-to-government sale. But they should have seen Trump’s next move coming.

People close to Trump—it’s still not clear who—suggested to the Qataris that instead of selling the plane, they could donate it to the United States. A gift. A freebie from “friends” who had already put hundreds of millions of dollars into Trump’s son-in-law’s private-equity firm and bought a debt-laden Manhattan hotel belonging to Steve Witkoff, his Middle East special envoy, for $623 million. That’s to say nothing of the $8 billion they’d spent to build the Americans an air base—the biggest U.S. military base in the Middle East—or their plans to spend $10 billion more to enhance and maintain it. What was another $400 million, for a plane that the president so dearly loved?

Even some Qatari leaders were surprised by the president’s gall. But they did what they’ve always done when an American official has asked them for something dubious—politically, ethically, or even legally. They said yes.

It’s not easy to buy good press, though the Qataris have tried. But it also takes real effort to generate the kind of bad press the plane brought to a country whose name many Americans probably can’t pronounce correctly (it’s kah-tar). The bipartisan outrage in Washington was incandescent. The plane was a flying emolument, an obvious constitutional violation. “Only a FOOL would not accept this gift on behalf of our Country,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. But what Trump couldn’t, or wouldn’t, see is that only a fool would view the plane as anything other than a massive bribe, especially given that Trump said publicly that he planned to have it transferred to his presidential library once he leaves office.

Even by the immoderate standards of the Persian Gulf, it’s quite a move to give a world leader a free airplane. But the Qataris had already given one to the president of Turkey, and they saw that bad press dissipates. And as the Qataris know, probably better than anyone, the price with Trump is always high.

To understand this strange deal—so absurdly corrupt that there is nothing analogous in the history of the American executive branch—it’s necessary to understand Qatar, the rare country with both the means and the disposition to even contemplate it. The Qataris don’t have allies. They have investments. Their investments in American relationships are undoubtedly their most important, and they’ve provided billions of dollars of diplomatic and military-support services to the U.S. But at the same time they’ve been providing money to America’s defense, they’ve also provided support to America’s enemies.

The Qataris play every side, and many of their partners resent them for it. Nonetheless, for decades their experience seemed to show that they really could just buy their national security, along with global influence and even a cosmopolitan culture. Trump must initially have seemed to them to be an ideal partner. And indeed, just four months after the delivery of his airplane, in September 2025, the president signed an executive order that ostensibly guaranteed American protection.

But recently, Qatar’s leaders haven’t gotten what they paid for. In February, the United States attacked Iran with practically no warning to the Qataris, despite the fact that they host a major U.S. military base. Then Iran attacked Qatar, badly damaging the country’s natural-gas facilities, the main source of its wealth. Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, the only route available to Qatar to export its natural gas, which must be liquefied for transport and is complex to deliver. The country’s neighbors can move oil over land and are planning to build new pipelines now that Iran controls the waterway. But Qatar is stuck, uniquely afflicted by the misadventures of the guy who took their airplane.

In Trump, the Qataris had met a man who could not be bought. He could be paid, and expected to be. But the security the Qataris hoped for turned out to be a protection racket. A man who doesn’t remember yesterday never asks Are we friends? He only wants to know, What have you done for me lately?

Qatar would never have had so much to lose had it not won the geological lottery. In 1971, engineers with Shell who were prospecting for oil 50 miles off the coast came upon a promising Triassic-period limestone formation about 200 feet below the ocean surface. To their surprise, it turned out to contain natural gas.

Subsequent mapping revealed that the gas field was not merely large. It was gargantuan—roughly twice the size of Delaware. So much natural gas was seeping out of the ground that previously unknown species of bacteria had evolved just to consume it. In this one continuous structure was 20 percent of the world’s known natural-gas reserves.

The deposit was a one-of-a-kind bounty. Thanks to their oil reserves, which were modest for the region, the Qataris were already rich. But the North Field, as the new gas deposit became known, made them unfathomably so. It took 25 years and a meaningful chunk of Qatar’s wealth for the country’s ruling Al Thani family to develop the field. Recently, annual liquefied-natural-gas revenue has been roughly $50 billion, which accounts for about a quarter of Qatar’s gross domestic product.

Younger Qataris wouldn’t recognize the country their grandparents inhabited in their youth. It was a poor and forgettable protuberance on the east coast of Saudi Arabia before large oil shipments began in the mid-20th century. Pearl diving accounted for much of its economy. Now the government pays for Qataris’ health care throughout their lives. It pays for their higher education, having imported universities from the U.S.: Georgetown, Northwestern, Carnegie Mellon, and other colleges have branches there, supported by Qatari largesse. Qataris pay no income tax, and foreign residents, who make up 90 percent of the country’s 3.3 million people, do just about all of the physical labor. You are unlikely to see a Qatari behind a cash register, driving a taxi, waiting on a table, or picking up a piece of litter. (Thanks to the foreign workers who perform the most menial tasks, you are also unlikely to see much, if any, litter on a Qatari street.) And now, with all the money in the world, the Qataris have extended their influence well beyond their borders.

The Qataris have been drawn to trophy real estate and major international events, such as Formula 1 races and the World Cup, which Qatar hosted in 2022 under a cloud of allegations (all denied) that they had bribed the selection committee. When it won its bid, Qatar didn’t even have stadiums in which to play the matches. The Qataris built them, of course, seven in all, along with new roads and public-transportation systems. Well, they didn’t. Migrant laborers did the work, and thousands of them died, according to human-rights organizations. Undeterred by scandal or by summer temperatures that often reach 120 degrees, last year Qatar announced its bid to host the Olympic Games in 2036.

In London, the Qataris’ state investment fund owns Harrod’s, the Shard (Western Europe’s tallest building), a portion of Heathrow Airport, and about a quarter of the district of Mayfair, also known as Little Doha, in the city’s center. In France, it has the Paris Saint-Germain Football Club, and in Washington, it holds a minority stake in the Wizards, the Capitals, and the Mystics. In New York, it’s got the Plaza and St. Regis hotels and a stake in the Empire State Building.

Qatar is also the world’s largest acquirer of fine art. The country’s collection of paintings and sculptures is estimated to be worth $40 billion, advisers who helped amass it told me. The works, which include some of the most expensive paintings ever sold at auction, are destined for museums that Qatar is still constructing.

But more than buildings, art, or global sporting events, Qatar invests in relationships, and one above all others. When Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani overthrew his father to become emir in 1995, he told the American ambassador that he wanted Qatar to be the United States’ most valuable ally in the Gulf. This was an audacious proposal from a 43-year-old ruler who imagined that his upstart emirate had anything to offer the world’s remaining superpower. But Hamad and the favorite of his three wives, Sheikha Moza bint Nasser, had a shared vision for Qatar to become a modern nation, rooted in traditional Muslim culture, and they needed a protector. After the September 11 terrorist attacks, the United States’ large military presence in Saudi Arabia became untenable. The Americans needed a new military base, so Hamad gave them one.

Al Udeid Air Base, located southwest of Doha, is now home to about 10,000 U.S. military personnel, as well as the Middle East headquarters of U.S. Central Command. Its runway, more than two miles long, can accommodate heavy cargo planes, aerial-refueling tankers, and fully loaded B-52 bombers.

The Qataris performed other services, too, becoming a diplomatic back channel for the United States to communicate with extremist groups, including the Taliban and branches of al-Qaeda. They hired retired U.S. military officers and diplomats whom they’d worked with as lobbyists and advisers. In 2022, after Qatar helped evacuate U.S. personnel from Afghanistan, President Biden called it a “good friend and reliable and capable partner.” To label this partnership an alliance would be overselling each side’s contributions, and Biden’s comments glossed over the times when Qatar was less than reliable. The relationship was mostly transactional from the start. But for two decades, it worked, by and large, for both sides.

“I trust Qatar like I trust a rest-stop bathroom,” the inimitable Senator John Kennedy, a Republican from Louisiana, told Fox News not long after Trump’s airplane deal was announced. One of his Republican colleagues, Mike Rounds of South Dakota, likened the plane to a Trojan horse, citing security concerns.

Their worries weren’t solely based on the gift of the airplane. The Qataris spend lavishly on their friends, but they have also broadly defined who counts as one. For decades, Doha has provided support of one sort or another to some of the very groups that the United States has tried to eradicate.

In the mid-1990s, Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the future architect of the September 11 attacks, worked in a Qatari government ministry while plotting terrorist attacks against the United States. He fled the country after a member of the ruling family, who Mohammad later said had paid for some of his jihadist activities, reportedly tipped him off to an FBI manhunt. One former U.S. official told me that when the CIA was searching for Osama bin Laden after the 9/11 attacks, the Qataris obtained information about his communications and potential whereabouts but declined to share everything they knew about the origins of that information with the Americans.

Qatar has had diplomatic relations with Iran for more than 50 years. Its approach has been partly pragmatic—about a third of the massive natural-gas field that Qatar depends on lies in Iranian territory. But its steady engagement is unusual in the region and a major irritant to Qatar’s neighbors.

Hamad’s regime cultivated ties to the Muslim Brotherhood and anti-Israel clerics, including one who famously praised suicide bombers. In the mid-’90s, Qatar established and funded Al Jazeera, creating a media network putatively free from state censorship but that reliably railed against Israel. And in 2012, the emir became the first head of state to visit Gaza since Hamas had violently taken power five years earlier. He brought $400 million in reconstruction aid. That year, Hamas also moved its political headquarters from Damascus to Doha. The country’s strong embrace of a group designated as a terrorist organization in the U.S. sets it apart from other Muslim monarchies, just as its stance toward Iran does. During the Obama administration, U.S. officials publicly put the Qataris on notice for lax financial regulations that made their banking system a useful money-laundering network for extremists and terrorists.

The many U.S. intelligence officers, diplomats, and military veterans I spoke with consistently offered the same appraisal: It would be inaccurate to say that Qatar directly “supports terrorism,” but the country’s money and politics support an environment that helps terrorism and extremism flourish.

The Qataris justify their involvement with a wide range of regional players by saying that they are a small country, beset by chaos on each side, that cannot afford to make many enemies. They say that active outreach puts them in position to help solve conflicts within the region, and even outside it. Since the late ’90s, their diplomats have acted as mediators, negotiators, and go-betweens for violent political disputes, proxy battles, and full-on wars in Lebanon, Yemen, Darfur, and more. Qatar has been involved in talks between rival Palestinian factions, between Chad and Sudan, between the U.S. and, respectively, the Taliban, Venezuela, and Iran. Last year, Qatari officials told me, their teams were participating in a dozen separate negotiations at once.

“You can literally draw a small circle around Qatar, where an oasis of stability exists,” Majed Mohammed al-Ansari, an adviser to the prime minister and the chief spokesperson for the foreign-affairs ministry, told me not long ago. “And even that oasis keeps shrinking.” The alternative to trying to tamp down surrounding flare-ups, he said, is “basically watching your house burn down while drinking tea.”

Qatar has sometimes been called “the Switzerland of the Middle East,” but it isn’t. Neutrality is the cornerstone of Swiss foreign policy. (The country didn’t even join the United Nations until 2002.) Qatar funnels money to some of the parties whose conflicts it tries to resolve—sometimes it is paying both opposing parties in one way or another—and it takes political positions that neutral countries avoid.

Much of the country’s mediation and back-channeling has benefited the U.S., and some has come at its behest. Qatari officials are quick to point out that the American government asked them to host Hamas, so that Washington could open an indirect channel with its leaders. This is true, up to a point. Washington had concluded that Qatar was likely going to let Hamas move in anyway, after the group was expelled from Syria. “We did ask, but it was like pushing on an open door,” a former U.S. official who was serving at the time told me.

What skeptics in Washington call duplicity, Qatar calls a balancing act. Regardless of what you call it, building and maintaining relationships with dubious actors has turned out to be, in itself, a source of influence and leverage. It also, some Qataris admitted to me, helps keep the ruling family from becoming targets of terrorists.

Above all, the Qataris hedge their bets. They are morally flexible rather than rigidly ideological. True, some conservative Islamists in the government have embraced extremists and bridled at Qatar’s rush into modernity. But they have also failed to stop it. The country’s relationships are not passionate; they are tactical and serve the national strategy: to be safe, to have influence, and to remain very, very rich.

Trump must have seemed a gift to the Qataris when he was first elected in 2016. Here was an unashamedly acquisitive leader who showed plenty of ideological flexibility where there was a deal to be done. But the indications that he might care little about Qatar’s preexisting relationship with the U.S. came early and were hard to miss.

On May 23, 2017, the Qatar News Agency’s website and social-media feeds published comments attributed to Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, who had succeeded his father as emir four years earlier, praising Hamas and Hezbollah, Iran’s regional proxy militia. Tamim reputedly cautioned other nations not to confront Iran, which he called an “Islamic power.”

There is persuasive evidence that the Qatari sites were hacked and the emir’s comments faked. But Qatar’s neighbors were incensed, and on June 5, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, and Egypt simultaneously severed diplomatic ties with Qatar. They expelled Qatari citizens and closed land, air, and sea routes to the country, disrupting imports overnight. The tiny nation was blockaded.

At a dire moment like this, Qatar might have expected that its strategic investment in the United States would pay off. But Trump encouraged the blockade. Barely six months into his first term, he had just wrapped up a summit with Arab leaders in Riyadh, his first trip abroad as president, where he awkwardly swayed in a ceremonial sword dance and laid hands with the Saudi king on a strange glowing orb. Trump gave a major speech about combating terrorism. As the blockade took hold, he went on Twitter:

So good to see the Saudi Arabia visit with the King and 50 countries already paying off. They said they would take a hard line on funding extremism, and all reference was pointing to Qatar. Perhaps this will be the beginning of the end to the horror of terrorism!

It’s doubtful that Trump understood the nuances of terrorist financing in the Middle East. But he had done business with the Saudis as a private citizen. A Saudi prince had bought Trump’s yacht in the early 1990s, when he was a real-estate developer deep in debt and in need of cash. And during the presidential campaign, Trump had registered eight companies that, based on their names, appeared set up for a potential hotel deal in Saudi Arabia.

Trump’s friends in Riyadh had just moved against the host of the United States’ biggest Middle Eastern military base. Despite American grievances about Qatar’s support for extremism, it’s very hard to imagine that another president would have green-lighted the blockade.

Qatar, of course, had resources available to weather the crisis. To guarantee that its residents would have enough milk and yogurt, for instance, the government flew in more than 3,000 dairy cows from Europe, Australia, and California aboard Qatar Airways. The government subsidized a new farm in the desert, and within two years Qatar was a dairy exporter.

By late 2019, Qatar and its neighbors were quietly talking, and tensions eased. The Trump administration, by then, was in a hurry to confront Iran and wanted a united front in the Gulf. The Americans urged the parties to reconcile. Qatar took effective measures to clean up its banking system, a long-sought U.S. objective. And in August 2018, an asset-management company in which Qatar was a major investor announced it had agreed to lease a Manhattan office building owned by Kushner Companies for more than $1 billion, saving the family business of Trump’s son-in-law from debt. The crisis in the Gulf officially ended in 2021, when Qatar and its neighbors reestablished diplomatic ties.

Trump had burned the Qataris with his support for the blockade, but he’d come back around. And the whole episode seemed to reaffirm the idea that with Trump in charge, the power of money was ascendant. Certainly, Qatar started acting more nakedly on that premise.

Since Trump was first elected, Qatar has paid nearly $250 million to at least 88 different lobbying and public-relations firms in the United States. Washington is steeped in influence peddling, but Qatar’s largesse is out of proportion for such a small country. It has hired several officials and advisers in Trump’s orbit—to do what, other than be a friend of Qatar, is not always clear. FBI Director Kash Patel and former Attorney General Pam Bondi received payments from Qatar before joining the current administration. (As AG, Bondi reportedly signed a memo saying the Qatari plane transfer was legal.) White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles was a co-chair of a public-affairs firm that lobbied on behalf of the country.

Qatari cash sloshes across the political aisle. The country’s advisers have included staff members who worked for Senator Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the foreign-relations committee, as well as the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, Trump’s friend and frequent golfing buddy.

From 2021 through June 2025, Qatar’s agents officially reported 627 in-person meetings with U.S. political contacts, more than any other country. Many of them were with Graham, who lambasted Qatar for its support of Hamas “and other terrorist groups” after the October 7 attacks, but later called Qatar “our allies” after Qatar Airways announced it would purchase up to 210 Boeing Dreamliners assembled in Graham’s home state of South Carolina.

Qatar throws lavish parties in Washington and flies politicians, journalists, and social-media influencers to Qatar every year for the Doha Forum, covering their first-class airfare and five-star-hotel accommodations. In May 2025 at the Qatar Economic Forum, another marquee event where the country tries to showcase its influence and convening power, the news about Trump’s new airplane had just broken. The prime minister seemed annoyed during an onstage interview. “I don’t know why people are thinking about it as a bribery or consider it as Qatar wants to buy influence with this administration,” Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani said, without evident irony. “We need to overcome this stereotype,” he added, that Qatar tries to buy influence in the U.S.

The next month, Iran attacked Qatar for the first time. More than a dozen short- and medium-range ballistic missiles targeted the American military base in a largely performative retaliation for U.S. air strikes on Iran, which Trump claimed, falsely, had “obliterated” its nuclear facilities.

Then, in September, Israel launched an air strike on Hamas’s political office in Doha, killing six people, including a Qatari security official. The country could now claim the unenviable distinction of having been attacked by Iran and Israel in the same year.

The Qataris got a little payback: Trump was furious because he had been angling for a Nobel Peace Prize for ending the war in Gaza, and cease-fire negotiations, facilitated by the Qataris, had been under way. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was screwing up his plans. Trump claimed not to have known that the strike on Qatar was coming and tried to get Qatari diplomats back to the negotiating table. He insisted that Netanyahu apologize to his Qatari counterpart. In front of photographers, Netanyahu called the prime minister from the Oval Office and read from a script partly written by Ali al-Thawadi, a Qatari fixer, who watched the scene from a chair near the Resolute Desk.

For a time, it seemed like Qatar would get more still from the attack, and from its long and expensive cultivation of Trump and his allies. The same day as Netanyahu’s apology, Trump issued an executive order that any attack on the “territory, sovereignty, or critical infrastructure” of Qatar would be considered a threat to the peace and security of the United States. To go with that security guarantee, the Defense Department announced that Qatari fighter pilots would train at a U.S. air base in Idaho.

But like all of Trump’s guarantees, this one didn’t amount to much. After the U.S. and Israel again began attacking Iran on February 28, despite efforts by Qatar and other governments in the region to prevent the war, Iran struck the main natural-gas processing facility in Qatar. The energy minister said that the damage reduced export capacity by 17 percent, a hobbling blow to the economy.

The attack followed an Israeli strike on an Iranian natural-gas plant, and as with Israel’s earlier air strike on Doha, Trump claimed not to have known about it in advance. Officials in Doha were furious again, and this time they were frightened. Qatar’s entire relationship with Iran, which lay at the core of so many of its disputes with its Gulf cousins, was premised on pragmatic coexistence. Trump’s war was breaking that peace.

Between Iran’s missile attack and its closure of the Strait of Hormuz, the only transit point for Qatari gas, the country has had little choice but to shut down its liquefied-natural-gas production entirely since the war began. The lifeblood of the nation’s ambitions, plans, and influence is drying up. And Qatar’s global strategy, premised on so many contradictory bets, is crumbling. It’s hard to say these days who ranks higher on the list of threats to the emirate: Israel, which has long been Qatar’s main adversary; the United States, its most important strategic partner; or Iran, which controls the strait for the foreseeable future.

During a two-month period this summer, while the American president declared the war in Iran over, then back on again, Iran continued to strike Qatar. On America’s 250th birthday, the president’s new jet flew low over Washington, part of an all-day aviation spectacle that shook the walls and windows of houses in the capital, including mine. The retrofit had reportedly cost more than $1 billion, two and a half times the Qataris’ initial asking price. But the president seemed to think he’d gotten what the country had paid for. The jet was “the largest and the greatest in every aspect,” a “flying White House at a level of luxury no one has ever seen before.”

As the plane heads off to a hangar, to be retrofitted again for the security features it needs to protect the commander in chief, Qatar’s negotiators sit in Doha trying to find an off-ramp between the Americans and the Iranians. The middleman is stuck in the middle—right where they always put themselves.

entries.title: Party in the (Downwardly Mobile) U.S.A.
entries.summary: The mainstream is disintegrating. What’s a frustrated pop star to do?
entries.content:
The mainstream is disintegrating. What’s a frustrated pop star to do?

With every passing year, Miley Cyrus’s 2009 single “Party in the U.S.A.” comes to feel more like an artifact of an empire before its fall. When the Disney Channel star sang about hopping off the plane at LAX with a dream and a cardigan—on the way to turn her country-girl ambitions of fame into Hollywood reality—she projected an image of a nation that still believed in its own myths, trusted its power centers, and grooved together to the same songs. The guitars fizzed like a fresh can of Coke, and Cyrus advertised to the world’s strivers that making it in America is a breeze.

Released less than a year after the 2008 financial crash, “Party in the U.S.A.” was part of a crop of songs that have, in recent years, been labeled “recession pop.” It’s an affectionate term for happy, uncomplicated anthems—think Katy Perry’s “Teenage Dream” or the Black Eyed Peas’ “I Gotta Feeling”—that once distracted from headlines about bailouts and foreclosures. The optimism of those songs now seems rarer in American life, but over the past few years, TikTok pundits and media commentators have theorized that a new wave of recession pop might come “back” to suit the economic weirdness of the mid-2020s.

I’ve never really bought that argument, for a few reasons. Perky pop largely faded from the charts in the mid-2010s not because of the national mood but because of changes in how people listen: Streaming eroded the top-down distribution channels, such as radio and network TV, that loved to broadcast sugary, universally appealing sing-alongs. More audience-segmented styles—country, hip-hop, confessional bedroom songwriters—now rule the charts. So-called pure pop has become a subculture, almost akin to indie rock.

And what’s been happening lately in that subculture is more interesting than a mere revival of carefree times. This summer has served up a slate of great party songs that are full of twisted nostalgia and tarnished glamour. Pop is dancing in the ruins of the American dream—or at least in the ruins of the traditional record business.

“Party in the U.S.A.” came to mind while I was listening to “Ain’t in LA,” a tasty new single by the rising star Adéla. She is a 22-year-old Slovakian musician who learned English by watching Hannah Montana, and the song is an obvious Cyrus homage. It revisits the trap-pop sound of Cyrus’s 2013 hit “We Can’t Stop” and features that song’s deep-voiced rapper, Theron Thomas. The breezy, yelled chorus seems designed to, as Cyrus put it in ’09, make the butterflies fly away. But the track has a naggingly wistful undercurrent—and its lyrics flip “Party in the U.S.A.” on its head.

The verses describe the yearnings of a young girl with Madonna and Destiny’s Child posters pinned to her wall. She wants to be a star—but watching American media taught her that “her dreams don’t live at home.” Then the chorus booms a corrective: “It’s all a lie / The baddest bitches ain’t in LA.” In the music video, Adéla balls out in stereotypical ways—twerking, joyriding, writhing on top of a pile of gold trophies—in her hometown of Bratislava, alongside kid dancers in Slovakian folk garb. She has a message for “girls in them unknown cities”: It’s hot to stay put.

Adéla would know. As a teenager, she traveled to Hollywood in hope of a big break on the 2023 reality show The Debut: Dream Academy. A co-production of Geffen Records and the Korean firm Hybe, the series recruited young women from around the world to audition to be part of a girl group subjected to the rigorous management style of K-pop. A trained ballerina with a fierce pout, Adéla performed strongly—but after she was criticized for not perfectly gelling with the other performers, she became one of the first girls cut from the running.

Dream Academy represented the response of the U.S.’s faltering star-making machine to international competition. Over the past decade or so, K-pop has become the premiere global source of the sort of polished dance-pop that homegrown stars such as Beyoncé and Backstreet Boys once specialized in. Dream Academy sought to repurpose the K-pop model for performers who sing mostly in English and come from all over. The resulting band, the sextet Katseye, has put out a string of hyperactive, utterly frivolous songs—full of L.A. references to $20 smoothies and trysts in Bel Air—that have performed decently on the U.S. charts. But the continuing viability of this carefully stage-managed project is an open question: Two Katseye members are on hiatus for health-related reasons.

Adéla, meanwhile, has embarked on a solo career that’s made her the connoisseur’s choice for girlish bangers. Although “Ain’t in LA” sounds clean and sleek, her earlier singles were a bit edgier, pairing dark electronica elements with lyrics about surviving the record industry’s manipulations. Her penchant for minor chords and meta-commentary recalls early Lady Gaga, but whereas that star subsumed her personal identity into operatic symbolism, Adéla’s music remains human-scale—bruised by rejection and panting with yearning. “Staring at a TV screen ’til I got bloody eyes / Just a little European girl, was plotting on my rise,” she squeals in “KGB,” sounding like someone whose childhood dreams have begun to smolder into a hunger for vengeance.

An even grimier sense of desperation powers the most astonishing pop song of the year: “BEAT UP CHANEL$,” by the 29-year-old singer-songwriter Slayyyter. On paper, it could be part of the Broadway tradition of “I want” songs— this one sung by a character who covets MTV-typical treasures such as money, drugs, and handbags. But Hamilton this isn’t: Amid a clanging guitar and bass, Slayyyter screeches those desires like a caged fox. The track cycles between wild accelerations and gliding comedowns, gaining tornadic intensity. When a cheerful melody pops up at the end of the song, the effect is as life-affirming as stepping onto the platform after a terrifying roller-coaster ride. “I want something for real,” goes the final refrain.

This gonzo song represents a culminating statement for an artist who’s been hustling for years. In the late 2010s, Slayyyter began to attract online attention for putting a deconstructed, sinister spin on Y2K pop. When I interviewed her in 2021, she told me about being a teen girl in suburban St. Louis who was radicalized by the media’s harsh treatment of Britney Spears and Paris Hilton. Chasing stardom in the early 2020s, she moved to L.A. and recorded two dance-pop albums, themed around the horrors of fame, that pleased fans but received little attention more broadly. She’s said that she went into the studio for her third studio album, this year’s WOR$ST GIRL IN AMERICA, with the assumption that it would be her last.

She thus let herself indulge extreme impulses: scuzzy production inspired by obscure artists from her old iPod, feral lyrics delivered in what she’s called a “tweaker twang” tone of voice. Many tracks seem to be about her own failure as a celebrity—“I’M ACTUALLY KINDA FAMOUS” is a glorious parody of the D-list mindset—and the album’s music videos have shown her back in her native Missouri, partying in tattered jeans among trailer parks. But though the album documents a breakdown, it has turned out to be her breakthrough. Released in March, WOR$ST GIRL IN AMERICA debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot Dance Albums chart, drew her some big festival audiences, and earned her the fandom of Courtney Love. The buzz seems to still be growing: This month, Slayyyter scored her first-ever entry on the Hot 100.

The track to achieve that feat is a sister song to “BEAT UP CHANEL$,” titled “brand new chanel$.” It’s entirely different from its predecessor but nearly as good: a blurry reimagining of the crisp, uplifting pulse of circa-2010 electronic dance music and pop punk. As with “Ain’t in LA,” a surprising amount of vulnerability lies beneath the song’s spiky attitude. Slayyyter sounds heartbroken about a cheating ex whose new woman, she sighs, wants brand-new Chanels—a villainous desire in a cultural moment when destroyed seems better than new.

The urge to defy a mainstream that’s corrupted and fake has long been, of course, one of music history’s great drivers of progress. In trying to contextualize the sound that Slayyyter and her internet-pop peers in the share, Pitchfork just coined the fun term hyperclash. The name suggests a hybrid of the subgenres hyperpop (2010s laptoppers, many of them queer, subverting formulaic catchiness with video-game-inspired chaos) and electroclash (a late-’90s and early-2000s scene of ironic techno with punk influences). The writer Anna Gaca theorizes that hyperclash artists are drawn to hedonistic noise “as a protective adaptation amid the endless horrorscroll.”

But if a trend is unfolding, it also involves pop musicians reckoning with the death of pop itself. Just as fans have lately become obsessed with the concept of the “flop,” artists are treating the archetype of the world-conquering superstar as an unattainable myth from a not-so-distant past. Singers who once projected glitz are having a blast with the aesthetics of downward mobility.

The acclaimed but under-the-radar singer Tinashe, for example, is promoting an album called Popstar. Her latest single is a trippy house song, “Melatonin,” that accuses people of “sleeping on” her—ignoring her greatness—and whose video is set in what looks like a foreclosed mansion. (In another single, the slinkily paranoid “Crash Out,” she sings, “The American dream is outdated.”) An equally telling example: Kim Petras, a 33-year-old German who’s spent years making bright and bland pop with the notorious producer Dr. Luke, recently went independent and put out her most experimental—and best—album yet, Detour. Her persona used to be that of a Malibu socialite. Now, on the swooning “Jeep,” she fantasizes about driving around gas-station parking lots, drinking Four Loko, and doing “middle-American shit.”

None of these artists is rejecting the race for riches; we aren’t back in 2013, when Lorde mocked the “Cristal, Maybach, diamonds on your timepiece” she heard about on the radio. Rather, the mood is one of thwarted materialism, of wanting but not getting. And no one should mistake much of this wave for a meaningful rebellion against the industry. Adéla works with Capitol Records; Slayyyter joined Columbia Records to put out WOR$T GIRL IN AMERICA. At a time when even the biggest stars seem a little niche, major-label backing doesn’t quite mean what it once did—but clearly, music’s power brokers have judged that a scuffed-up, striving sound might appeal to the public right now.

It’s not difficult to see why. After a long pop-cultural swing away from Millennial do-goodery toward a redux of 1980s “greed is good” aesthetics, burnout with chasing the bag is finally setting in. Many influencers are starting to see their reach wane; luxury brands are facing flatlining sales. At the same time, anti-institutionalist sentiment—whether directed at political parties, Big Tech, or the entertainment business—is at a high. “Party in the U.S.A.” landed at a time when people still regarded Hollywood as a land of magic, not as a playground for sex traffickers.

The most popular songs of late reflects these trends as well. Ella Langley’s record-setting charts run with “Choosin’ Texas” speaks to a demand for music that’s indifferent to the cosmopolitan hustle. The stateside appeal of non-English-language stars also represents shifting ideals of what success looks and sounds like. Just as Adéla advises that the baddest bitches ain’t in L.A., Bad Bunny scoffs at the idea that Puerto Ricans need to head to the mainland United States to make their dreams come true.

In these conditions, it’s no wonder that pop, once the sound of the center, is finding glamour in marginality. Stars who might otherwise aspire to godhood are meeting listeners where they’ve always been: partying in their own backyard, with their own friends, and on their own terms—even while dreaming of something bigger.

entries.title: Is Mojtaba Khamenei Dead?
entries.summary: The office of Iran’s supreme leader has fallen quiet, fueling uncertainty in a country with decisions to make.
entries.content:
The office of Iran’s supreme leader has fallen quiet, fueling uncertainty in a country with decisions to make.

Last Tuesday, Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei hosted a wake for his father and predecessor, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. Among the thousands who thronged Tehran’s biggest mosque were the country’s most prominent political figures and several of the elder Khamenei’s sons. One person was notably absent: Mojtaba, the event’s official host.

Almost six months since his anointment, Iran’s supreme leader has been entirely obscured from the public eye. Not a single contemporaneous picture, video, or audio recording of him has been released. Many of the country’s top political leaders admit that they haven’t seen him—among them Abbas Araghchi, Iran’s foreign minister and a member of the National Security Council. IranWire, a London-based opposition outlet, reports that not a single cabinet member has met with Mojtaba since he became supreme leader.

Not even Mojtaba’s close friends and relatives have seen him. Fewer than five people have met with Mojtaba since his ascent to power, Mohammad Hossein Khoshvaght, a former official and a relative of Mojataba’s told me, “due to security precautions.”

The rationale is not implausible. Mojtaba would be a likely target for an Israeli or U.S. air strike, such as the one that killed his father. Direct communication from him could supply Iran’s enemies with clues to his whereabouts. He is also said to have sustained injuries in the February strike on his family that have made public speeches and appearances difficult.

But the totality of Mojtaba’s invisibility and a recent decline in statements from his office have set Tehran abuzz with new rumors of his death. Some sources inside and close to the government speculated to me that Mojtaba recently died from the injuries that he had sustained in February. And irrespective of his actual status, the uncertainty might have major implications for Iran.

“I believe Mojtaba has either passed away or is brain-dead,” a staffer at a government institution in Tehran told me, citing the tailing off of even indirect communication from the leader to the outside world. At least two other government officials told me the same. One said that he believed Mojtaba died or became brain-dead earlier this month.

Two sources in the Iranian government recently told IranWire that word had spread among those at the “highest level of the regime” that Mojtaba was doing very poorly and could die at any moment. About two weeks ago, a public appeal went out on a domestic messaging service, asking Iranians to pray for Mojtaba’s health and sacrifice sheep to bless him, as is customary in Islam. Mojtaba’s life was “under threat,” and some “clerics” had warned that he might be killed, the appeal said.

Since he was appointed, Mojtaba has ruled by decrees disseminated by his office. Iran’s supreme leader is a religious authority in addition to being the head of state, and on July 27, Mojtaba’s office published a list of his answers to practical questions posed by the devout. One correspondent had requested guidance on eating with bleeding gums, because blood is haram—forbidden—in Islam. Any food contaminated with blood, including from one’s own gums, must be thrown out, Mojtaba ruled. If his office is to be believed, then the leader was well enough to ponder Islamic law and issue relevant rulings as recently as a month ago.

The office’s most recent statement came on August 9 and reported that Mojtaba had met with President Masoud Pezeshkian. It didn’t say when the meeting had taken place but noted that it was on the occasion of the president’s third year in office, which puts it on or after July 28. Pezeshkian confirmed to the Iranian media that he spent seven hours with Mojtaba discussing the war and the country’s beleaguered economy. (According to Khoshvaght, Pezeshkian was taken to that meeting “without knowing where it was,” which suggests that he was transported blindfolded, mafia-style.) Also on August 9, Mojtaba issued a slew of decrees, appointing several generals to top military positions and swapping out one of his representatives on the National Security Council. Since then, the office has been silent.

Khoshvaght assured me that Mojtaba is definitely alive. The rumors about the leader’s death are “part of a psychological war hoping to demoralize Iran’s officials and its people, for them to give up to the pressures and threats of America,” he said. He added that the rumors also aim to embolden Iranians opposed to the regime, giving them “courage to come to the streets so that the plans of the U.S. and Israel can be realized.” Abdolreza Davari, a former adviser to the interior ministry and a vocal supporter of Mojtaba’s, told me that the leader is “in full health” and will soon be revealed to the public. But the two weeks with no communication, the public appeal for sheep sacrifice, and the rumors emanating from government circles have led many Iranians to doubt such assurances.

Whether Mojtaba is dead or alive, his public absence creates problems for the Iranian regime. The supreme leader holds most of the constitutional power in the Islamic Republic and has in the past served as the final arbiter among the system’s warring factions and institutions. Mojtaba appears to be sitting these conflicts out, at a moment when their outcome could be particularly consequential.

The country’s 13-person National Security Council is effectively running the country as a collective. It is chaired by Pezeshkian, a reformist who favors an end to the war with America, and includes Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the powerful parliamentary speaker who led the talks with the United States. But it also includes General Ahmad Vahidi, the head of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, and other military leaders.

Back in June, 12 of the council’s 13 members voted in favor of the memorandum of understanding that Iran reached with the United States in Islamabad. Mojtaba sent a message endorsing the deal but also noting that he had initially opposed such an agreement “in principle.” Hard-line critics of diplomacy seized on this to claim that Ghalibaf had usurped power and forced the memorandum on the leader. A news outlet linked to a faction in the IRGC even issued a documentary called Ghalibaf’s Coup.

Mojtaba neither endorsed this view nor put it to rest. Rather, he has remained mum as various factions have purported to speak for him. Pezeshkian has told reporters that in his meeting with Mojtaba, the leader stressed that regime officials should “keep unity and cohesion” and avoid infighting.

But the infighting goes on. In June, a statement signed by 63 of the 88 members of the Assembly of Experts, a clerical body tasked with supervising the supreme leader, admonished regime officials that none of them was authorized to act against Mojtaba’s “definite opinion.” At the same time, the statement called on any Muslim “who could gain access” to kill Donald Trump—not quite the message of Iran’s negotiators, but rather more consonant with Mojtaba’s statements promising “blood revenge.”

The Iranian regime has existential choices to make as it decides between diplomacy and conflict. Iran’s constitution is clear about who has the authority to set the country’s course. But no one seems able to say for sure whether that person is alive or dead. And without a firm hand at the top, indecision can become a purgatory without a foreseeable end.

entries.title: The Jews Who Voted for Hitler
entries.summary: What happened when members of a minority community cast its lot with a political leader who despised them
entries.content:
What happened when members of a minority community cast its lot with a political leader who despised them

On the evening of February 5, 1930, the art and theater critic Paul Fechter took the podium before the League of Nationalist German Jews, in Berlin, to discuss purported Jewish control of the press and the arts in the country. “When Dr. Max Naumann invited me to give a lecture in your circle, I rather impulsively said yes,” Fechter began. “When he then told me the topic he wanted me to address, my immediate reaction was: Good grief ! One could not have found a better topic for making oneself thoroughly unpopular and for antagonizing everyone in the room.”

For too long, Fechter said, people had been too “shy, fearful, cautious” to speak openly about the Jews. Fechter, an editor at the conservative newspaper Deutsche Allgemeine Zeitung, was pulling no punches. The popular Jewish humorist Kurt Tucholsky, Fechter said, had insulted the German people with his recent book, Deutschland, Deutschland über alles, an acid satire about the army, the police, the civil service, the national anthem, even Sekt, a popular sparkling wine.

“A large portion of the literary and art worlds are in Jewish hands,” Fechter continued. “The theaters, the major publishing houses, the major art dealers are all at least partially under Jewish control.” Jewish art dealers, Fechter said, filled their galleries with works by “Manet and Monet and Renoir and Gauguin and Picasso and Cezanne”—French Impressionists and Modernists, in other words, rather than traditional German painters. The Antigermanismus among Jews, Fechter declared, was “far more robust” than the Antisemitismus among right-wing German nationalists.

Naumann, the founder of the league, published the Fechter tirade in his monthly publication, The Nationalist German Jew, circulated to his group’s 7,000 members, mostly middle-class professionals in more than 20 chapters around the country. Naumann himself was a Berlin-based Jewish attorney who was decidedly antidemocratic, belligerently nationalistic, and unapologetically critical of other Jews.

He blamed Ostjuden—the “Eastern Jews” fleeing pogroms in Russia, Romania, Austria, Hungary, Poland, and elsewhere—for flooding the country with unwanted immigrants. He felt pity but no solidarity. “It is the same pity we feel when there is talk of the Turks massacring Armenians or of lynch mobs targeting black people in America,” Naumann wrote—an abstract pity without emotional connection. In his league’s founding treatise, On Nationalist German Jews, published in 1920, Naumann had compared Zionists, those seeking a Jewish homeland in Palestine, to Nazis, whose political movement had just been founded. “Both groups, the fanatics of Zion and the knights of the swastika, are basically the same in that they have turned a question of ancestry into a question of nationality,” Naumann argued.

Naumann defended his German and Jewish identities in equal measure, a stance reflected in the term nationaldeutscher Jude—a blood-and-soil German Jew.

Naumann drifted right with the rest of German politics in the early 1930s, first abiding and then supporting the extremist, right-wing, rabidly anti-Semitic positions of Adolf Hitler. It is impossible to imagine a more tragically misplaced political calculation than Naumann’s embrace of national socialism. Though the Hitler Juden—or Nazi Jews, as Naumann’s adherents came to be known—represented less than 2 percent of Germany’s half-million Jews, they provide a cautionary tale of members of a minority within a minority who cast their lot with a political leader who openly despised them.

Naumann was born in 1875 into a middle-class family—bankers, landowners, cloth merchants—in an era of unprecedented opportunity for German Jews. They had recently gained the right to vote. They could run for office. They enjoyed equal protection under the law. Professions formerly restricted were now open—law, medicine, academia. Naumann studied jurisprudence at the Friedrich Wilhelm University of Berlin, where he joined a fraternity and was given a Schmiss across his chin, the honorific dueling scar of a true Prussian. But prejudice persisted.

When Naumann was denied an officer’s title in the Prussian military because of his Jewish heritage, he enlisted in the 2nd Bavarian Infantry Regiment. Naumann advanced through the ranks, from lieutenant to first lieutenant and eventually to captain, serving with distinction during the First World War. He was awarded an Iron Cross First Class and an Iron Cross Second Class, among other decorations, for “outstandingly brave deeds performed in the face of the enemy that went far beyond the call of duty.”

But Jewish veterans of the Great War returned to find Jews collectively vilified for Germany’s defeat and surrender. The Reich Federation of Jewish Front-Line Soldiers countered with an information campaign highlighting their commitment and sacrifice—100,000 Jewish soldiers had served at the front; 35,000 had been decorated for bravery; 12,000 had given their lives for the fatherland. The Central Association of German Citizens of Jewish Faith, or Centralverein, sought to combat rising anti-Semitism through legal protections of Jewish identity and heritage. Meanwhile, the Zionist Federation of Germany urged German Jews to immigrate to Palestine for their own safety.

Naumann found these responses wholly inadequate or misguided. He denounced the members of the Centralverein as ineffective “Dummköpfe,” or idiots, and the Zionists as traitors, foremost among them “the world-famous scholar Einstein,” who placed his Jewish identity over his German heritage. “The spiritual and even the material misery of the Jews in Germany would never have assumed such frightening proportions,” Naumann claimed in 1927, “if steps had been taken in time to prevent the Zionists, and especially the Zionist Ostjuden, from positioning themselves before Jews and non-Jews alike as the only rightful spokesmen of Judaism.”

Naumann believed that anti-Semitism needed to be “dismantled,” not legally challenged, the Centralverein’s preferred approach. During the war, Naumann had watched anti-Semitic sentiment evaporate in the heat of battle, where what mattered, he later recalled, were “actions,” not “words,” and where “a tough, resilient, determined willingness to put one’s head on the line” for comrades and the fatherland “transcended all class and racial difference.” This was the experience that shaped his approach to German politics.

He was joined by Alfred Peyser, the chair of the League of Nationalist German Jews, who was also an eminent physician and the municipal counselor of an upscale Berlin district. In a foundational 1922 essay defining the concept of a “nationalist German” Jew, Peyser warned fellow Jewish Germans against returning to “Ghettoknechtschaft”—enslavement to the ghetto—or trying to escape to “Zion,” urging them instead to embrace the “German fatherland.” “Yes, we love this land, its language, its people,” Peyser wrote. “We feel as one with it!”

Naumann and Peyser found a powerful ally in Samuel Breslauer, the editor of the Berliner Lokal-Anzeiger, a popular conservative newspaper. Breslauer traveled to New York City in the spring of 1927 with a delegation of German newspaper editors to meet with their American counterparts, including Adolph Ochs, the publisher of The New York Times. Breslauer advocated for fierce German nationalism and equally fervent Judaism. He defended this duality in an article titled “Me, an Antisemite.” “If over the course of three decades I have undergone a change,” Breslauer wrote, it had been a political drift to the right—but “certainly not” away from Judaism. Instead, he insisted, his Judaism had deepened and strengthened—“in the religious, not in the ethnic-national sense.”

Naumann had initially aligned his league with the German People’s Party, a center-right party led by the Nobel laureate Gustav Stresemann. But the political picture changed in September 1930, when the National Socialists surged nearly tenfold in national elections. Fascism was suddenly fashionable. Siegfried “Fred” Bon, the Jewish author of a three-volume philosophical treatise, Does 2 x 2 = 4?, sought to square Judaism and national socialism. In a January 1931 article for The Nationalist German Jew, Bon cataloged Jewish contributors to the country’s conservative movements, foremost among them Walther Rathenau, a foreign minister in the Weimar Republic and the first person, according to Bon, who’d sought to merge nationalism with socialism—“the very positions that today constitute the foundations of the National Socialist program.” Bon’s article appeared under the title “Can Jews Be National Socialists?”

Naumann, for his part, suggested that they could be, and he pointed to Italy as evidence. Jews had joined Benito Mussolini in the 1922 March on Rome. Guido Jung, a Jew, was Italy’s fascist minister of finance. Renzo Ravenna, a Jew, was the fascist mayor of Ferrara. When Girolamo Bassi, a Jewish lawyer in Venice, faced financial difficulties, a judge suggested that he join Mussolini’s Partito Nazionale Fascista. “So, two months later, my father became a cardcarrying Fascist,” Bassi’s son Roberto later recalled, “and having bought a fine black uniform went with the others to demonstrate support for Il Duce.”

Naumann attributed the fascist receptiveness toward Jews in Italy not only to the absence of Zionists and Ostjuden in that country but also to Jews’ absence from “intellectual” professions. Naumann urged young German Jews to pursue careers in trades such as carpentry and masonry rather than professions such as law and medicine. “Of the approximately 200,000 Jews in Italy, at most 10% are doctors, lawyers, and journalists,” The Nationalist German Jew reported in a 1933 article titled “Why There Is No Hatred of the Jews in Italy.” (Although it’s true that there was less anti-Semitism in Italy than in Germany, the article’s premise would be proved grimly wrong when Italy passed a series of discriminatory racial laws starting in 1938 and deported Jews to Nazi extermination camps.)

In July 1932, Naumann caused a sensation when he appeared to urge German Jews to vote National Socialist in the upcoming Reichstag elections. In an article in Fechter’s newspaper, Naumann claimed that national socialism was the only viable future for the country—“that here, and only here, a path is being forged that can lead to a rebirth of Germanness and to the restoration of German prestige.”

Centralverein was outraged. An op-ed in the organization’s newspaper, Central-Verein-Zeitung, lambasted Naumann for inaccuracy and irresponsibility, and argued that to discount the threat posed by Nazi anti-Semitism was absurdly credulous. Whatever common values Naumann shared with Hitler—anti-communist, antirepublican, antidemocratic—hatred of Jews remained foundational to Nazi ideology. Central-Verein-Zeitung reminded Naumann of the Nazis’ “unbridled attacks” and “public incitement” against Jews, noting that “Herr Hitler has never, on any occasion, contradicted the speakers of his own party regarding their stance on the Jewish question.”

But Naumann continued to believe that the heated rhetoric against the Jews was political posturing that would cool once Hitler was in office, and once the inciting political effects of Jewish Communists, socialists, and Zionists had been neutralized. A trove of about 11 million digitized National Socialist records, analyzed by an international group of scholars from Harvard and elsewhere in a National Bureau of Economic Research paper published last April, includes 580 personal statements by Nazis, given in 1934, explaining their reasons for joining the party. Fully 26 percent of these Nazis cited their dislike of Jews as an “explicit causal reason” for joining the party, which suggests that anti-Semitism was considerably more than an incidental element of the party’s ideology. But Naumann was fixated on the other motivations for joining the party, which are reflected in the scholars’ analysis of these statements: 63 percent cited a hope for national renewal and the restoration of public order, while 53 percent expressed a desire for social belonging, 49 percent the need to combat communism, and 29 percent the belief that the party could lift them out of economic hardship. Naumann’s fatally naive view was that if these other concerns could be addressed, anti-Semitism would be diminished.

Following Hitler’s appointment as chancellor, in January 1933, anti-Semitic violence spiked horrifically. Jews were assaulted on the street, at their places of business, in their homes. One young man was lashed bloody, then had pepper rubbed in his wounds to heighten the agony; he died of sepsis. An apartment on Berlin’s fashionable Friedrichstrasse was repurposed as a torture room, its walls spattered with blood.

The foreign press chronicled the atrocities prominently. On March 25, Hermann Göring, the powerful Nazi cabinet minister, summoned Naumann and other Jewish leaders to his office. Göring read from a stack of foreign-newspaper clippings with growing fury. “Unless you put a stop to these libelous accusations immediately,” Göring said, “I shall no longer be able to vouch for the safety of the German Jews!” Naumann had intended to use the meeting to protest the rising anti-Semitic violence; to that end, he confronted Göring with a list of attacks on Jews. But he left the meeting as a propagandist for the Third Reich. “While we readily acknowledge that there are excesses against German Jews,” Naumann declared in a public statement, “we are not interested in foreign interference in our internal affairs.”

To his fellow Jews of German heritage, Naumann counseled patience. “Today we are enduring without question days of rage,” he wrote in May. “It was inevitable that this anger—built up and heightened over fourteen years—would initially erupt in an explosive outburst.” But Naumann anticipated the day, “in the not too distant future,” when the country’s anti-Semitic fever would break and “Aryan and Jew” would once again “join hands” in common cause for the fatherland. “When this day of self-reflection finally arrives,” Naumann wrote, “that will be the beginning of the real answer to the German Jewish question.”

The preceding month, however, Hitler’s government had enacted the Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service, which banned “non-Aryans” from government posts, as well as the Law on Admission to the Legal Profession, which prevented Jews—including Naumann—from practicing law. The Law Against Overcrowding in German Schools and Universities, passed at the same time, restricted the enrollment of Jewish students.

Amid these draconian measures, Hans Heinrich Peyser, the son of Alfred Peyser, ran into Naumann one day on the Berlin subway. Naumann was just returning from a meeting with leaders of the Nazi storm troopers. He spoke to Peyser of the Nazis’ “high ideals” and the need to try to understand things from their perspective. “I found this excessive self-absorption and inward-looking preoccupation, in light of what had already happened in Germany, to be absolutely grotesque,” Peyser wrote.

The Jewish Telegraphic Agency, in New York, a wire service covering the global Jewish community, viewed Naumann and his adherents with similar dismay. “Although their professions have been taken away from them, and although they live in a state of rigid suspense and fear of the moment when they will be humiliated, beaten, or imprisoned, a large number of German Jews continue to remain faithful to the fatherland,” the agency reported on August 13. The report noted Naumann’s denunciation of Zionists as “traitors to their country.”

Stories circulated of “Naumann Jews” ending their meetings with Hitler salutes and the singing of “Horst Wessel Lied ,” the Nazi Party anthem. Though Naumann dismissed the alleged singing as “Jewish horror stories,” he defended the stiff-armed salutes and the presence of Nazi banners, saying that Jews needed to “overcome their fear of the swastika”: “After all, the Christian cross,” he wrote in April 1934, is also a symbol “in opposition to Judaism,” but “for a long time now no reasonable Jew has refused to accept the Iron Cross or other cross-shaped decoration.”

In August of that year, when Reich President Paul von Hindenburg died, Naumann urged Jews to approve a public referendum transferring Hindenburg’s powers to Hitler in his capacity as chancellor, effectively handing Hitler unchallenged dictatorial rule. (He did so despite acknowledging to his fellow Jews that the Nazi regime had “brought rigors to us.”) “We urge all Jews who feel themselves Germans to vote ‘Yes’ on Aug. 19,” Naumann declared.

Naumann reaffirmed his solidarity with Hitler’s government the following week, when he dispatched a telegram to the Nazi leader informing him that the League of Nationalist German Jews would not be attending a conference in Geneva for the establishment of the World Jewish Congress. Learning of this, Pariser Tageblatt, a newspaper for anti-Nazis in exile, responded: “Thank God!”

A Gestapo report on a meeting of 400 nationalist German Jews in Berlin on May 27, 1935, confirms that Naumann’s support for Hitler persisted. Naumann “emphasized in particular that the members considered themselves genuine Germans,” the report noted, and “had welcomed the transformation in Germany brought about by the Führer.” The meeting ended with a rousing chorus of “Deutschland, Deutschland über alles.”

For all Naumann’s efforts to win approval or recognition from Nazi leaders for his organization, or for his view on what Jews’ place in the Third Reich should be, he never received any.

On September 15, 1935, Hitler’s government introduced the Reich Citizenship Law and the Law for the Protection of German Blood and German Honor, collectively known as the Nuremberg Laws, stripping Naumann and half a million other Jewish Germans of their citizenship. By then, Naumann was divorced, and his daughter had broken irreparably with him over his pro-Nazi position.

On November 18, Naumann’s league was forcibly disbanded. Naumann himself was arrested by the Gestapo that same day and taken to Columbia-Haus, an SS detention and torture facility. A few weeks later, after attempting to commit suicide by slitting his wrists with the glass from his spectacles, Naumann was released. He died of cancer in May 1939, isolated and abandoned.

By that point, thousands of Jews had escaped abroad. Alfred Peyser was stripped of his medical license and briefly incarcerated before immigrating to Sweden in 1939, where he survived the war. Other Naumann Jews were not so fortunate. Siegfried “Fred” Bon was dispatched to the Theresienstadt concentration camp in September 1940; he was executed there in April 1944. Samuel Breslauer, who lost his editorial post and his property to the Nazis, also perished in Theresienstadt, along with his wife, Bertha.

Naumann’s remains were interred in a Protestant cemetery in the town of Stahnsdorf, southwest of Berlin, where his headstone still stands.
